     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Operations
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs, unless the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given (see Critical Rules). Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window. For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation:
     96	
     97	- Only the recorded symptoms, findings, observations and gaps reach the investigation summary. Text in a chat message or a later mitigation plan does not, so put the verdict and the recommendation in the findings.
     98	- Write the symptom with its impact: the alarm name, threshold and breaching datapoints, whether the alarm has actions, and the onset time.
     99	- Write the root cause finding description as a complete answer on its own, in this order:
     100	  1. "Binding layer: `<layer>`." in those words.
     101	  2. The numbers that prove it: the exceeded checks (minutes at 1), per-volume demand against the volume limit, and the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes against the instance EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, for example "500 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s, the provisioned throughput".
     102	  3. The recent history: alarm episodes, modification history, and whether earlier peaks stopped at the same ceiling.
     103	  4. "Recommendation (proposal, not executed; it runs only after an operator approves it on the approval card):" the exact command with the target, how the target was computed, the next limit after the change, and the EBS baseline of the next larger instance size when the instance becomes the next limit.
     104	  Do not leave the conclusion or the target only under Gaps or in a later message.
     105	- Record each piece of evidence as an observation and link every observation that supports a finding to it, so each finding shows its supporting observations. This includes the limits table, the instance layer check, the volume status result and the history.
     106	- Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.
     107	- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Record a gap that applies to the whole answer once.
     108	
     109	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, keep it as the verdict and write "Binding layer: Indeterminate" with the answer to the user's question first. Then present a short list of candidate causes, as described in [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). For each candidate, give the supporting observations with numbers and the specific check that would confirm it or rule it out. Merge overlapping candidates, and name a candidate that the data rules out as ruled out, with the numbers. Do not name AWS-side impairment as the cause, and do not call the pattern an impairment pattern. Give the customer the detailed performance statistics step from [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) to run during the symptom.
     110	
     111	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     112	
     113	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     114	
     115	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     116	
     117	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     118	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The answer says "Binding layer:" followed by the layer, and gives the four exceeded checks as minutes at 1 or "no datapoints". A performance verdict has the limits table: per-volume demand next to the volume limit, summed demand of all attached volumes next to the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS, which one binds, and the exact target with its computation.
     119	- A performance verdict states the recent history: the alarm history, the modification history (latest record and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or a Gap), and whether the same pattern happened earlier.
     120	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     121	- An Indeterminate verdict says "Binding layer: Indeterminate", answers the user's question first, and lists the candidate causes, each with its supporting observations and the check that confirms or rules it out, without overlapping candidates or the same gap repeated under each one.
     122	- In an investigation, the root cause finding (or, for Indeterminate, the first finding) carries the verdict, the numbers, the history and the Recommendation, because only findings reach the summary.
     123	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first. The first lines of a snapshot answer name every snapshot with its tier and the evidence for it.
     124	- Every proposed change follows [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals): exact command, expected effect, modifications left in the 24-hour window, rollback, and the approval statement.
     125	- When a volume modification is in progress, the answer states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window, each one completing before the next, and the count used from AWS CloudTrail or a Gap.
     126	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     127	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     128	
     129	---
     130	
     131	## Critical Rules
     132	
     133	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval, and the reply says so in those words whenever the user types an approval. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).
     134	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     135	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.
     136	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     137	- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources, and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs.
     138	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     139	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     140	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     141	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     142	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     143	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.
     144	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     145	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     146	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     147	
     148	## Gotchas
     149	
     150	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     151	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     152	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     153	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     154	- When the instance is the binding layer, do not call the volume saturated, even when its idle time is near 0. Say that its I/O is waiting on the instance limit.
     155	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     156	- `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, and no datapoints is not the same as 0. The instance checks `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with `InstanceId`.
     157	- Amazon EBS detailed performance statistics are read on the instance, not through an AWS API. They are a step the customer runs; the agent never runs them.
     158	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     159	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     160	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     161	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     162	
     163	## Error Handling
     164	
     165	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     166	
     167	## References
     168	
     169	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     170	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     171	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     172	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     173	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     174	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     175	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     176	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     177	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     178	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     179	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "134775d2-31dc-42e5-8c63-07c17abd341e", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_Vwk3Fy087ztULR0gmZcjdW", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history with `DescribeAlarmHistory` for the last 24 hours: when it first entered ALARM, and any earlier ALARM and OK transitions. Report earlier transitions as history, because they show whether the pattern recurs.
     17	- Describe the impact in the symptom: the alarm name, metric, threshold, the datapoints that breached it, whether the alarm has actions configured, and the onset (the minute the metric left its normal level, for example "queue length rose from about 0 at `<time>` to 1.5 from `<time>`").
     18	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     19	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.

     124	
     125	### Micro-bursting
     126	
     127	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.
     128	
     129	Check the exceeded checks from Step 2a first. If the checks are 0 or have no datapoints and the question is still open, give the customer the detailed performance statistics step below.

     131	### Detailed performance statistics (a step the customer runs)
     132	
     133	Amazon EBS NVMe devices on Nitro instances keep detailed performance statistics that the customer reads on the instance, at up to 1-second granularity, for any volume type, at no extra cost.      156	### Volume initialization after restore
     157	
     158	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized. Check `DescribeVolumes` `SnapshotId` and `CreateTime`.      160	### Burst credits
     161	
     162	- Volume level: gp2, st1 and sc1 publish `BurstBalance`. Draining or at 0 means the volume has dropped or will drop to its baseline. Recommend gp2 to gp3 migration, or a size or type that gives the needed baseline.
     163	- Instance level: some smaller instance sizes publish `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`. Draining or at 0 means the instance has dropped or will drop to its EBS baseline. Recommend an instance type whose baseline covers the measured demand.
     164	
     165	### How much IOPS or throughput to provision
     166	
     167	1. Measure peak demand per volume over a representative window (IOPS and MiB/s, Step 3 math).
     168	2. For io1 and io2, check that the IOPS value also gives the throughput limit the workload needs.
     169	3. Check the instance's remaining EBS baseline: baseline minus the measured usage of the other attached volumes.
     170	4. Propose the smaller of the measured need and what the instance can deliver. If the need exceeds the instance baseline, say so and recommend an instance type change.

     5	## Elastic Volumes rules
     6	
     7	- You can make up to 4 modifications to a volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change).

     9	- A modification request cannot be cancelled after it is submitted.
     10	- States are `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed` (or `failed`). In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies, and performance is between the source and the target. The modification completes on its own.
     11	- Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.

     3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.
     9	3. **Binding layer.** One of: Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, Indeterminate, Not applicable.
     10	4. **Recommendation.** Exact parameters (volume ID, dimension, target value, how the target was computed), or "No change". Mutating steps are proposals for a directed action, written as described in [Change proposals](#change-proposals).
     11	5. **Separate findings.** Other true facts, labelled so they never change the Answer. For example a modification that succeeded on a volume whose instance caps delivered IOPS: the cap goes here, never as "the modification failed".
     12	6. **Gaps.** What could not be checked and why (API denied, approval gate, metric absent).
     13	
     14	## Limits table for performance verdicts
     15	
     16	Every performance verdict puts the numbers side by side in one table under Evidence, so the reader can see which limit binds without doing the arithmetic. Use the values measured in this session, with the time window.
     17

     20	| Volume `<id>` IOPS | `<n>` IOPS | provisioned `<n>` IOPS | `<n>` IOPS | Yes or No |

     57	An Indeterminate verdict is a short list of candidate causes, not a single sentence. The Binding layer stays Indeterminate, and the answer says so in those words: "Binding layer: Indeterminate".
     58	
     59	Start with the answer to the user's question and the reason, for example "Binding layer: Indeterminate.      79	
     80	| Candidate | Check that confirms it or rules it out |
     81	|---|---|
     82	| A slowdown in the Amazon EBS storage path that the checks have not flagged | `DescribeVolumeStatus` (status and the I/O performance check, which covers attached io1, io2 and gp3 volumes), `VolumeStalledIOCheck` (1 means failed), AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 in the Region and Availability Zone. Recheck while the symptom lasts. If it persists with all checks clean, escalate to AWS Support with the evidence pack |
     83	| Injected latency from a fault injection experiment | AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment with `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io` that targets the volume or instance |
     84	| A change in the workload's I/O pattern (larger I/O, more random I/O, more writes) | Average I/O size and the read and write split before and during the alarm window, from `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeReadOps` and `VolumeWriteOps` |
     85	| The instance EBS limit, shared with the other attached volumes | Summed IOPS and MiB/s of every attached volume, including the root volume, against the `DescribeInstanceTypes` baseline; `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck`; `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%` |
     86	| A cause outside Amazon EBS on the instance (application locks, file system, CPU) | `CPUUtilization` and the attribution matrix below. OS-level data such as `iostat` is outside this skill, so ask the customer for it |
     87	| Volume initialization after a restore from a snapshot | `DescribeVolumes` `SnapshotId` and `CreateTime` |
     88	| Volume or instance limit, including sub-minute bursts | The limits table and the four exceeded checks. When demand is far below every limit and the checks are 0, title it as ruled out. The customer can confirm with the [detailed performance statistics](troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) |
     89	
     90	Close with what to watch (AWS Health Dashboard, volume status checks, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`), the detailed performance statistics as a step the customer runs during the symptom, and when to escalate.
     91	
     92	In an investigation, record this as findings so the summary carries it:
     93	
     94	- The first finding is titled with the verdict and the answer, for example "Binding layer: Indeterminate. Adding IOPS will not help", and its description gives the reason with the numbers, the clean direct signals, what to watch and when to escalate.
     95	- Each candidate is its own finding. Link to it the observations that support it or rule it out, so each one shows its supporting observations.
     96	- Link a gap only to the candidates it affects. A gap that applies to everything (for example "the values were given by the user, not read from the APIs") is recorded once and not repeated under every candidate.
     97	
     98	When the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given, build the candidates from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs. Describe the impact from the given values (percent of each limit in use, time each unit of queue adds, average I/O size) instead of writing that it is unknown.
     99	
     100	### Qualitative attribution matrix for "is it storage?"
     101	
     102	From the attribution draft, with the numeric CPU bands removed because no public source states them.
     103	
     104	| CPU | Volume latency | Queue length | Likely attribution |
     105	|---|---|---|---|
     106	| High | High | High | Application drives heavy I/O. Both compute and storage are stressed |
     107	| High | Normal | Low | Compute, not storage |
     108	| Low | High | High | Storage. The application waits on I/O. Go to the decision tree |
     109	| Low | Normal | Low | Neither. Check network, locks and the application |
     110	
     111	"High" and "normal" mean compared with the same resource's own history and the type's documented expectation in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     112	
     113	## Change proposals
     114	
     115	Every mutating change (`ModifyVolume`, an AWS KMS key or key policy change, a quota request, an instance type change) is a proposal. Include all of these:
     116	
     117	1. **Whether the change will help,** from the measured data. If the data shows it will not help, say so first and say what will.
     118	2. **The exact call,** as an AWS CLI command with every parameter filled in from the APIs, for example `aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id <volume-id> --iops <target> --region <region>`. If the user named a target, give the command for that value. If a different value is better (for example the instance EBS baseline caps what the volume can deliver), also give the command for the recommended value and how it was computed.
     119	3. **Expected effect,** including the next limit (for example "the instance baseline of `<n>` IOPS then caps delivered IOPS").
     120	4. **For a volume modification:** the state sequence (`modifying`, `optimizing`, `completed`), the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window with each one completing before the next, and how many remain after this change from the AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` count (or say the count is unconfirmed and list it under Gaps).
     121	5. **Rollback,** as the exact reverse command and when it is possible (after the change completes for a volume, and it counts toward the 4; size cannot be reduced).
     122	6. **Cost direction,** with a link to the pricing page. Do not type a price.
     123	7. **The approval statement,** in plain words: "A typed approval in chat is not approval. This change runs only as a directed action that an operator approves on the approval card." If directed actions are not available in this Agent Space, say so and say that the customer can run the command above with their own credentials.
     124	
     125	Delete-class operations are never directed actions. Give them only as manual customer steps after the owner confirms.
     126	
     127	## Escalation (shared capability)
     128	
     129	Escalate to AWS Support when either is true:
     130	
     131	- Scope signals: an open AWS Health event for the volume, Availability Zone or Region; several resources failing the same way; `DescribeVolumeStatus` reports the volume as impaired or a failing status check.
     132	- A bounded investigation cannot explain the symptom: all layers below limits, no running AWS FIS experiment, no recent change, and the symptom persists.
     133	
     134	Specific cases:
     135	
     136	- Attach or detach stuck: the attachment stays in `attaching` or `detaching` and does not progress. Diagnose (instance state, device name, whether the volume is still mounted, any forced detach already tried), then contact AWS Support.
     137	- Modification in `optimizing` with `Progress` not increasing across several reads, or still optimizing after 24 hours. Tell the user the Amazon EBS User Guide says some performance changes take more than 24 hours, so this is a check, not a fault finding. Escalate with the evidence.
     138	- Snapshot stuck in `pending` with no progress change over the same kind of window.
     139	
     140	Evidence pack to include:
     141	
     142	1. Account placeholder, Region, volume IDs, instance IDs, snapshot IDs as read from the APIs
     143	2. The time window (first ALARM time, symptom start)
     144	3. Metric evidence with units (IOPS, MiB/s, latency, queue length, `EBSIOBalance%`, `BurstBalance`)
     145	4. Volume status and AWS Health results
     146	5. The latest `DescribeVolumesModifications` record per volume, and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events if that optional lookup was available
     147	6. What was ruled out and how
     148	7. The Gaps list
     149	
     150	## Review ratings
     151	
     152	Each review finding has:
     153	
     154	| Field | Values |
     155	|---|---|
     156	| Severity | `High`, `Medium`, `Low`, or `Indeterminate` (the data could not be read) |
     157	| Evidence | The values and API that show it |
     158	| Fix | A specific change with parameters |
     159	| Mutating? | Yes or No. Yes means the fix is a proposal for a directed action |
     160	
     161	Rate by impact if the risk happens, not by count. Severity guidance per area is in [review-operational.md](review-operational.md). The report layout is in [review-report-format.md](review-report-format.md).
     162	
     163	Every Review mode response MUST begin with the Summary table that rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection). The Summary table is required, not optional, and it comes before any per-area detail. Keep the six areas and the `High` / `Medium` / `Low` / `Indeterminate` scheme as written; do not invent new areas or ratings.

{"id": "1cee566439fc4c9db6a96143569dcdd9", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The limiting layer is the EBS volume. A steady write workload started around 18:07 UTC, when instance i-1234567890abcdef0_5 (c6i.xlarge) launched at 18:05. It sends about 1,000 write IOPS of 8 KiB each (about 8.2 MB/s) to io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0, which is provisioned at exactly 1,000 IOPS. In every 5-minute period from 18:10 to 19:25, the volume completed almost exactly 300,000 writes (1,000.0 IOPS) and no reads. That flat line is the volume's ceiling, not real demand: any extra requests wait in the queue. As a result, VolumeQueueLength stayed at about 1.5 against an alarm threshold of 1, and each write took about 1.49 ms. That matches the alarm and the slower application writes. The instance is not the limit: EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99%, both InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck read 0, and total instance IOPS (about 1,500) is far below the c6i.xlarge baseline of about 6,000. What to change: raise the provisioned IOPS on vol-0123456789abcdef0 with ModifyVolume, for example to 3,000–5,000. io2 allows up to 500 IOPS per GiB, so this 10 GiB volume can go to 5,000 IOPS without a size increase. The change takes effect online. One caution: instance EBS throughput is already about 139 MB/s, mostly roughly 131 MB/s of reads on gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_19, against an approximate c6i.xlarge baseline of 156 MB/s. That leaves little headroom, so if write throughput grows a lot, the instance's EBS bandwidth will become the next limit. In that case, cut the gp3 read load or move to a larger instance size.
## Evidence
- CloudWatch alarm example-a-io2-queue-length went to ALARM at 2026-11-23 18:11:04 UTC, with VolumeQueueLength at about 1.49–1.50 against a threshold of 1.0.
- EC2 DescribeVolumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is io2, 10 GiB, provisioned at 1,000 IOPS, and attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_5 as /dev/sdf.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteOps (5-minute Sum), 18:10–19:25 UTC: 300,000 in every period (1,000.0 IOPS, exactly the provisioned value). The 19:15 dip to 272,165 is the only exception. VolumeReadOps was 0.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteBytes: about 2.4576e9 per 5 minutes (about 8.2 MB/s). Divided by the write count, that is 8 KiB per write.
- AWS/EBS VolumeTotalWriteTime: about 448 s per 5 minutes across 300,000 writes, or about 1.49 ms per write. VolumeQueueLength averaged 1.47–1.50 from 18:10 to 19:10, after 0.86 in the 18:05 period when the workload began.
- AWS/EC2 for i-1234567890abcdef0_5: EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% held at 99% (minimum), and InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck were 0 for the whole window.
- AWS/EC2 instance totals: about 1,000 write and 500 read IOPS, plus about 131 MB/s of reads and 8.2 MB/s of writes (about 139 MB/s combined). That is well under the c6i.xlarge IOPS baseline and under its roughly 156 MB/s throughput baseline.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 1000 IOPS, 10 GiB)
- i-1234567890abcdef0_5 (c6i.xlarge)
- vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 (gp3, co-located heavy reader sharing instance EBS bandwidth)
- example-a-io2-queue-length (alarm)
## Gaps
- The volume-level VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck metrics returned no data, so the "pinned at the IOPS limit" conclusion comes from write counts sitting exactly at the provisioned value, not from a direct exceeded flag.
- The guest OS was not checked (iostat, queue depth, filesystem settings), so how much write demand the 1,000 IOPS cap is holding back is unknown.
- DescribeInstances reports EbsOptimized=false. c6i instances are EBS-optimized by default, and the instance metrics show it is not limited, but this was not checked further.
- The c6i.xlarge EBS baselines used here (about 6,000 IOPS and 1,250 Mbps / 156 MB/s) come from the published instance specs; I did not look them up again during this investigation.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "**Binding layer: Volume.** The io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 is held at its provisioned 1,000 IOPS. The instance still has headroom. To fix it, raise the volume's IOPS to 3,000. Everything below was read from the account in this session.

**What you're seeing:** The alarm `example-a-io2-queue-length` (VolumeQueueLength average above 1.0 for 3 of 3 one-minute points; no actions set) has been in ALARM since 18:11:04 UTC. That's about 80 minutes, longer than the 20 you mentioned. The queue rose from about 0 at 18:06 to about 1.5 from 18:08. It has run between 1.27 and 1.52 since. Write latency over the same period was 1.27–1.51 ms per write.

**Why the volume is the limit:**
- **Volume limit:**
  - From 18:08 to 19:32, the volume did a flat 1,000.0 IOPS. Almost all of it was writes, at 8 KiB each, which works out to 7.81 MiB/s.
  - `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` was 1 in 86 of 87 minutes (18:06–19:32). That check means the application asked for more IOPS than the volume is provisioned for.
  - `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` was 0 in all 87 minutes, so throughput isn't the problem.
- **Where the latency comes from:** with about 1.5 writes waiting at 1,000 IOPS, each write waits about 1.5 ms. That matches the measured latency. Unthrottled, io2 should be under 0.5 ms.
- **Instance has headroom:**
  - Both instance-level exceeded checks were 0 in 87 of 87 minutes.
  - The instance burst balances (`EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`) never went below 99%.
  - Across all attached volumes, the instance did 1,501.7 IOPS and 132.9 MiB/s. The c6i.xlarge baseline is 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s (149.0 MiB/s).
- **Not a fault or an experiment:**
  - Volume status is `ok` and the stalled-I/O check is 0.
  - There are no open AWS Health events for EBS or EC2.
  - The fault-injection experiment running in the account targets a different volume, not this one or its instance.
- **It has happened before:** the same flat 1,000 IOPS ran from 08:00 to 13:00 UTC today, with the exceeded check at 1 every hour. The alarm also fired at 07:43, 08:02–14:00 and 16:23–17:24. The volume has never been modified: no modification record, and no CloudTrail events on it in the last 24 hours.

| Layer | Demand | Limit | Binds? |
|---|---|---|---|
| io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0, IOPS | 1,000 (check at 1) | 1,000 provisioned | **Yes** |
| io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0, throughput | 7.81 MiB/s | 256 MiB/s (0.256 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS) | No |
| gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 | 500 IOPS, 125.07 MiB/s | 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s | At its own throughput limit (separate issue) |
| Root volume and vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 | about 1.4 IOPS, 0.01 MiB/s | — | No |
| Instance, all volumes combined | 1,501.7 IOPS, 132.9 MiB/s | 6,000 IOPS, 149.0 MiB/s | No (16.1 MiB/s left) |

**What to change** (this is a proposal and hasn't been run):
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
```
- **Why 3,000:** the instance baseline is 149.0 MiB/s. The other volumes use 125.08 MiB/s, which leaves 23.9 MiB/s. At 8 KiB per write that's about 3,060 IOPS, so 3,000 is the most that fits.
- **Limits it stays within:**
  - io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, so this 10 GiB volume could go to 10,000.
  - At 3,000 IOPS, the volume's own throughput limit becomes 768 MiB/s.
- **Next limit:** the instance's baseline throughput. At 3,000 IOPS the instance would use about 148.5 of its 149.0 MiB/s.
- **If you need more than 3,000:** either move to a c6i.2xlarge (12,000 IOPS and 312.5 MB/s, which is 298.0 MiB/s), or cut the read load on gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_19.
- **How the change applies:** it happens online and goes from modifying to optimizing to completed. The new IOPS already apply while it's optimizing.
- **Modification limits:** you can make up to 4 changes per volume in a rolling 24 hours, each finishing before the next. None have been used, so 3 would remain.
- **Rollback:** once it completes, run the same command with `--iops 1000`. That counts as one of the 4.
- **Cost:** provisioned IOPS cost more. See https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/.
- **Running it:** a typed approval in chat is not approval. This change runs only as a directed action that an operator approves on the approval card. {"type": "finding", "id": "rc-io2-iops-cap", "title": "io2 volume capped at its provisioned 1,000 IOPS", "description": "The binding layer is the volume. io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0 (example-a-io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 provisioned IOPS) ran a flat 1,000.0 IOPS from 18:08 to 19:32 UTC. Almost all of it was 8 KiB writes (7.81 MiB/s). VolumeIOPSExceededCheck was 1 in 86 of 87 minutes and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck was 0. About 1.5 queued writes at 1,000 IOPS means about 1.5 ms of wait per write, which matches the measured 1.27\u20131.51 ms. The instance (c6i.xlarge i-1234567890abcdef0_5) has headroom: both instance-level exceeded checks are 0, the EBS balances stay at 99% or above, and it runs 1,501.7 IOPS and 132.9 MiB/s against a 6,000 IOPS / 149.0 MiB/s baseline. Ruled out: volume faults (status ok, stalled-I/O check 0), AWS Health events (none), the FIS experiment (targets vol-1234567890abcdef0_11), and config changes (no modifications and no CloudTrail events on the volume). ## Results
I recommend raising provisioned IOPS on `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (io2, 10 GiB) from 1,000 to 3,000. This is a proposal only. I haven't run anything, and it runs only when an operator approves it on the approval card. A typed approval in chat is not approval. If directed actions aren't available in this Agent Space, an engineer can run the commands below with their own credentials.

The safety check accepted the plan on its third pass, with no remaining issues. The first two passes were rejected because the preparation phase had no real backup. Adding an EBS snapshot before the change fixed that.

**Why this helps:** the volume is the limit. It ran at exactly 1,000 IOPS (100% writes, 8 KiB average I/O, 7.81 MiB/s) and its IOPS-exceeded check was at 1 in 86 of 87 minutes (18:08–19:32 UTC). The instance, `i-1234567890abcdef0_5` (c6i.xlarge), had headroom: both instance EBS exceeded checks were 0 in 87 of 87 minutes and EBS balances stayed at or above 99%. The same 1,000 IOPS ceiling also held from 08:00 to 13:00 UTC today. The volume isn't impaired, so adding IOPS is appropriate here.

**Current state, read just now:**
- **Volume:** io2, 10 GiB, Iops 1000, `in-use` on `/dev/sdf`. It has no modification record, so all 4 modifications in the rolling 24 h window are available.
- **Instance:** c6i.xlarge, running, us-east-1a.
- **Alarm:** `example-a-io2-queue-length` is still in ALARM, threshold 1.0.

**How 3,000 was chosen and what limits it next:**
- The c6i.xlarge baseline is 156.25 MB/s, which is 149.0 MiB/s. The other attached volumes use 125.08 MiB/s, leaving 23.9 MiB/s. At 8 KiB per I/O that is about 3,060 IOPS, so the target is 3,000.
- At 3,000 IOPS the volume would move about 23.4 MiB/s. All volumes together would then be about 148.5 MiB/s against the 149.0 MiB/s instance baseline. That margin is very thin, so the instance becomes the next limit.
- In IOPS terms, the total would be about 3,502 against the instance's 6,000.
- If more is needed, the next size up (c6i.2xlarge: 12,000 IOPS, 312.5 MB/s = 298.0 MiB/s) is the way forward. io2 allows up to 10,000 IOPS on 10 GiB.

## Execution plan

### 1. Prepare
1. **Record the current configuration so it can be restored.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,State:State}'
   ```
   Expected: io2, 10, 1000, `in-use`.
2. **Take a snapshot of the volume first.**
   ```
   aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "Pre-change backup before IOPS 1000->3000" --region us-east-1
   ```
   - Note the returned SnapshotId.
   - Changing IOPS doesn't touch data. The snapshot is a safety net.
   - It adds a small snapshot storage cost.

### 2. Pre-validate (stop if either check fails)
1. **Confirm the volume isn't impaired.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volume-status --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   Expected: VolumeStatus `ok` and io-performance `normal`.
2. **Confirm no modification is already running.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   - Expected: `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound` (no record), or a `completed` record.
   - Stop if the state is `modifying` or `optimizing`.

### 3. Apply
**Raise provisioned IOPS from 1,000 to 3,000.**
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
```
- The change happens online, with no detach and no downtime.
- The state goes `modifying` → `optimizing` → `completed`. The new IOPS already applies during `optimizing`.
- This uses 1 of the 4 modifications allowed per volume in a rolling 24 hours. Each one must finish before the next starts, so 3 remain afterwards.
- Cost goes up, because io2 bills per provisioned IOPS. Pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/
- Risk: once the volume can deliver its full 3,000 IOPS, the instance EBS baseline (149.0 MiB/s) is almost fully used. Real write demand above 1,000 IOPS isn't known, because the old cap hid it.

### 4. Post-validate
1. **Watch the change complete.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetIops:TargetIops,Progress:Progress}'
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].Iops'
   ```
   Expected: TargetIops 3000, state `optimizing` or `completed`, Iops 3000.
2. **Check the metrics for about 15–30 minutes after the change.**
   - On `AWS/EBS`, with dimensions VolumeId=`vol-0123456789abcdef0` and InstanceId=`i-1234567890abcdef0_5`:
     - `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` should return to 0.
     - `VolumeQueueLength` should drop below 1.0.
     - `VolumeWriteOps` shows actual demand. If it settles near 3,000 IOPS, demand is still capped.
   - On `AWS/EC2`, with InstanceId `i-1234567890abcdef0_5`:
     - `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` should stay at 0.
     - `EBSByteBalance%` should not drain.
   - Write latency should fall below the incident's 1.27–1.51 ms/op.
3. **Confirm the alarm clears.**
   ```
   aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names example-a-io2-queue-length --region us-east-1 --query 'MetricAlarms[0].StateValue'
   ```
   Expected: `OK` after 3 one-minute datapoints with queue length at or below 1.0.

### 5. Rollback
**Return to 1,000 IOPS if the change causes contention at the instance level.**
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000 --region us-east-1
```
- This only works once the forward change is `optimizing` or `completed`.
- It counts as the 2nd of 4 modifications in the 24 h window.
- Rolling back brings the original ceiling and the alarm back. Use it only if instance throughput checks start firing.
- If the instance becomes the limit, the better fix is resizing to c6i.2xlarge, which needs a planned stop/start.

## Make the fix permanent
This setting predates any recent change, so whatever defines the volume should be updated. I don't know which repository or IaC tool manages it, so no URL is given.

- **What to change:** wherever `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (Name `example-a-io2`) is defined, set provisioned IOPS to 3000, so a later deploy doesn't quietly put it back to 1000.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### VolumeQueueLength above 1.0 on example-a-io2
**Description:** Alarm example-a-io2-queue-length (VolumeQueueLength average above 1.0 for 3 of 3 one-minute points; no actions) has been in ALARM since 18:11:04 UTC, about 80 minutes. The queue went from about 0 at 18:06 to about 1.5 at 18:08 and has stayed at 1.27–1.52 since. Write latency is 1.27–1.51 ms per write.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T18:08:00Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: io2 volume capped at its provisioned 1,000 IOPS
**Description:** The binding layer is the volume. io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0 (example-a-io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 provisioned IOPS) ran a flat 1,000.0 IOPS from 18:08 to 19:32 UTC. Almost all of it was 8 KiB writes (7.81 MiB/s). VolumeIOPSExceededCheck was 1 in 86 of 87 minutes and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck was 0. About 1.5 queued writes at 1,000 IOPS means about 1.5 ms of wait per write, which matches the measured 1.27–1.51 ms. The instance (c6i.xlarge i-1234567890abcdef0_5) has headroom: both instance-level exceeded checks are 0, the EBS balances stay at 99% or above, and it runs 1,501.7 IOPS and 132.9 MiB/s against a 6,000 IOPS / 149.0 MiB/s baseline. Ruled out: volume faults (status ok, stalled-I/O check 0), AWS Health events (none), the FIS experiment (targets vol-1234567890abcdef0_11), and config changes (no modifications and no CloudTrail events on the volume). The same cap recurs today: 08:00–13:00 and again from 16:00.
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **io2 volume pinned at exactly 1,000 write IOPS since 18:08:** From 18:08 to 19:32 UTC, vol-0123456789abcdef0 did a flat ~1,000.0 IOPS. All of it was writes, 8 KiB each (~7.8 MiB/s). That equals its provisioned IOPS. VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 every minute from 18:07. VolumeThroughputExceededCheck = 0 and VolumeStalledIOCheck = 0. Queue length stayed at ~1.48–1.51 and write latency at ~1.47–1.52 ms. From ~19:16, queue length fell to ~1.27 and latency to ~1.27 ms while IOPS stayed at 1,000. VolumeIdleTime also jumped from ~0% to 100%, which is inconsistent with sustained I/O.
- **Instance EBS limits not reached:** On i-1234567890abcdef0_5 (c6i.xlarge), InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck are 0 every minute from 18:06 to 19:32. EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stay at 99% (minimum). Total instance EBS traffic is ~1,500 IOPS and ~133 MiB/s, against a baseline of 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s. CPU is ~1%. The instance is not the I/O bottleneck, but its throughput headroom is small.
- **c6i.xlarge EBS limits far exceed the io2 provisioned IOPS:** c6i.xlarge is Nitro with EbsOptimizedSupport=default, so it is always EBS-optimized and EbsOptimized=false does not limit it. Baseline is 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s (burst up to 40,000 IOPS and 1,250 MB/s). The io2 volume is provisioned at only 1,000 IOPS. Three other volumes share the instance: two gp3 at 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s each, and the gp3 root.
- **Volume has repeatedly hit its 1,000 IOPS ceiling today:** Hourly data for vol-0123456789abcdef0: from 08:00 to 13:00 UTC it ran at 1,000 IOPS (7.8 MiB/s) with VolumeIOPSExceededCheck averaging 1.0 and queue length ~1.33. It was idle from 14:00 to 15:59, then the load resumed from 16:00 (exceeded check 0.68–1.0, queue 0.9–1.44). This matches the alarm's ALARM/OK transitions at 07:43, 08:02, 14:00, 16:23, 17:24 and 18:11. The alarm follows a recurring workload that saturates the provisioned IOPS, not a one-off fault.
- **FIS experiment targets a different volume:** FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (aws:ebs:volume-io-latency, 500 ms write latency on 100% of writes, 60 min) targets only vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, not vol-0123456789abcdef0. It also started at 19:32:35 UTC, well after the queue length alarm fired at 18:11. It does not explain the alarm.
- **No API changes on the io2 volume in the last 24h:** CloudTrail lookup by ResourceName vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 2026-11-22T19:30Z to 2026-11-23T19:35Z returned no events, so nobody modified or reattached the volume.
- **No AWS Health events for EBS/EC2:** AWS Health reports no open or upcoming EBS or EC2 events in us-east-1 for account 012345678901_1. This rules out a known AWS-side service event.
- **All 4 attached volumes report status ok:** describe_volume_status: vol-0123456789abcdef0, vol-1234567890abcdef0_19, vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 and the root vol-1234567890abcdef0_20 all show io-enabled=passed and io-performance=normal, with no events or actions. No volume modifications are in progress. None of the volumes was created from a snapshot except the root, and its initialization is complete. This points away from EBS-side impairment.

#### Gaps
- **Real IOPS demand above 1,000 is unknown:** The 1,000 IOPS cap hides how much the workload actually asks for. To measure it, run `sudo nvme amzn stats` on the /dev/sdf device twice during the symptom, a known number of seconds apart, and compare the growth in ebs_volume_performance_exceeded_iops.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise provisioned IOPS on io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 1,000 to 3,000

## Reasoning
The volume, not the instance, is the limit: a flat 1,000 IOPS of 8 KiB writes, with the IOPS-exceeded check at 1 in 86 of 87 minutes. The c6i.xlarge baseline (149.0 MiB/s) minus the 125.08 MiB/s used by the other volumes leaves 23.9 MiB/s, which is about 3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB, so the target is 3,000. The safety check accepted the plan on its third pass. It runs only when an operator approves it on the approval card; a typed approval in chat is not approval.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Record the current configuration so it can be restored (expected: io2…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,State:State}'
```
**Purpose:** Record the current configuration so it can be restored (expected: io2, 10, 1000, in-use)

#### 1.2 Take a backup before the change and note the SnapshotId
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "Pre-change backup before IOPS 1000->3000" --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Take a backup before the change and note the SnapshotId
**Advisory:** Small snapshot storage cost

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Confirm VolumeStatus ok and io-performance normal
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volume-status --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm VolumeStatus ok and io-performance normal

#### 2.2 Confirm no modification is running; stop if the state is modifying or…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm no modification is running; stop if the state is modifying or optimizing

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Lift the IOPS ceiling online, with no detach or downtime
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Lift the IOPS ceiling online, with no detach or downtime
**Risks:** Total instance EBS throughput nears 148.5 of the 149.0 MiB/s baseline, Real write demand above 1,000 IOPS is unknown, Uses 1 of the 4 modifications allowed per rolling 24 hours
**Advisory:** io2 bills per provisioned IOPS: https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm TargetIops 3000 in optimizing or completed state
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetIops:TargetIops,Progress:Progress}'
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].Iops'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm TargetIops 3000 in optimizing or completed state

#### 4.2 Confirm the cap is lifted without creating an instance bottleneck
**Type:** text
For 15–30 minutes, watch for: VolumeIOPSExceededCheck back to 0; VolumeQueueLength below 1.0; write latency below 1.27 ms; InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck and InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck at 0; EBSByteBalance% not draining. If VolumeWriteOps settles near 3,000 IOPS, demand is still capped.
**Purpose:** Confirm the cap is lifted without creating an instance bottleneck

#### 4.3 Confirm the alarm returns to OK
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names example-a-io2-queue-length --region us-east-1 --query 'MetricAlarms[0].StateValue'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the alarm returns to OK

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the original provisioning if instance throughput checks start…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original provisioning if instance throughput checks start firing
**Risks:** Only possible once the forward change is optimizing or completed, Brings the original ceiling and the alarm back, Uses the 2nd of 4 modifications in the 24 h window
**Advisory:** If the instance becomes the limit, resize to c6i.2xlarge instead (needs a planned stop/start)

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Set provisioned IOPS to 3000 in the volume's definition
**Description:** Wherever vol-0123456789abcdef0 (Name example-a-io2) is defined in IaC, set IOPS to 3000 so a later deploy doesn't put it back to 1000. The repository and tool are unknown.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The template says 3000
- A dry run against the live volume shows no difference
- Reapplying doesn't change IOPS

#### 2. Size IOPS from measured demand and the instance's EBS baseline
**Description:** Once the cap is gone, measure real write demand and base any further increase on the instance's EBS baseline, not just the volume.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Steady peak demand sits clearly below provisioned IOPS, so VolumeIOPSExceededCheck stays at 0
- If summed demand from all volumes approaches 149.0 MiB/s, the instance moves to c6i.2xlarge

#### 3. Alarm on VolumeIOPSExceededCheck
**Description:** Add an alarm (Maximum ≥ 1 for several minutes) for this volume and instance, with notification actions. The current queue-length alarm has no actions.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The alarm exists with actions and has been tested
